# How dbWise limits what an agent does to a database

This page explains the three levels, which layer guarantees what at each of them, what each level's
SQL policy admits, and why dbWise offers three SQL tools. For the exact commands, tools and texts,
see the [reference](reference.md). To set up roles that match the levels, see [Create the database
roles for dbWise](how-to.md#create-the-database-roles-for-dbwise).

## The three levels

An alias is a name the agent uses in a tool call. It has a level, `read` unless you say otherwise. A
call never does more than its alias's level allows.

| Level | What the agent can do | Login |
|---|---|---|
| `read` | Look at schemas and objects, and run SELECT and SHOW statements | The alias's `read` credential |
| `diagnose` | Everything at `read`, plus EXPLAIN with ANALYZE, health checks, top queries from `pg_stat_statements` and index advice | The `diagnose` credential for the diagnose tools; `read_sql` keeps using the `read` credential |
| `write` | Everything at `diagnose`, plus any SQL, committed | The `write` credential for `write_sql`; the other tools use the credential of their own level |

**The three levels as a ladder: each level can call the tools of the level below and adds its own**

1. `read`: schemas and objects, and SELECT and SHOW statements.
2. `diagnose`: everything at `read`, plus EXPLAIN with ANALYZE, health checks, top queries and index
   advice.
3. `write`: everything at `diagnose`, plus any SQL, committed.

Each level can name its own credential, so each can have its own database role. That is the point of
the split: the role that may read data, the role that may also look at other sessions' activity, and
the role that may change data are three roles, and you can revoke one without touching the others.

A call names an alias. It is allowed when the tool's level is at or below the alias's level, and it
connects with the alias's credential for the tool's level. `read_sql` on a `write` alias runs as the
`read` login under the `read` policy. A call that is refused for its level sends nothing to the
database.

### Which tools a level can call

Each row is a tool with its level (`any` for a tool without one) and the levels of the aliases that
can call it. With scripts on, a level chooser above the table marks the tools an alias at that level
can call.

| Tool | Level | Callable on aliases at |
|---|---|---|
| `list_databases` | any | read, diagnose, write |
| `reconnect` | any | read, diagnose, write |
| `list_schemas` | read | read, diagnose, write |
| `list_objects` | read | read, diagnose, write |
| `get_object_details` | read | read, diagnose, write |
| `read_sql` | read | read, diagnose, write |
| `explain_query` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `get_top_queries` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `analyze_db_health` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `analyze_workload_indexes` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `analyze_query_indexes` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `diagnose_sql` | diagnose | diagnose, write |
| `write_sql` | write | write |

## Where the guarantee comes from

At `read` and `diagnose`, the agent can change no schema, no data and nothing else that affects the
business: not other sessions, server configuration, statistics counters, replication consumers or
remote databases. Four layers hold that, and they are not equally strong.

1. **The database role.** It decides what the connection may do at all, and it is the one layer a
   statement in the session cannot switch off. A session can lift `default_transaction_read_only`
   and `statement_timeout` for itself, and it cannot grant itself a privilege. dbWise enforces this
   layer with the role gate: when a pool opens, the server runs one catalog query as the pool's role
   and refuses the alias when the role is a superuser, owns objects, holds a write grant, belongs to
   an application's role or can execute `dblink`. The rules are in [the
   reference](reference.md#the-role-gate). The role is where the guarantee for schema and data, and
   for reach into other sessions, rests.
2. **The SQL policy.** Every statement is parsed with PostgreSQL's own parser and checked before it
   is sent. Only statements of the level's kind pass, and every function call anywhere in the
   statement has to be in the level's function set: the check walks the whole parse tree, including
   `FROM` clauses, `ROWS FROM`, `LATERAL`, `VALUES` and CTEs. This layer stops the side effects that
   PostgreSQL lets a plain role execute by default: `pg_terminate_backend`, `pg_cancel_backend`,
   `pg_logical_emit_message`, `pg_advisory_lock`, `dblink_exec` and `set_config`. None of them is in
   the `read` or `diagnose` function set. The role recipe adds REVOKEs where the DBA can apply them.
3. **The read-only transaction and its ROLLBACK.** Every call at `read` and `diagnose` runs in a
   read-only transaction and ends with ROLLBACK. This is defence in depth: it stops DML and DDL
   hidden in views and functions, `nextval`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and `CREATE EXTENSION`. It
   holds because the policy refuses the statements that would make the transaction writable (`SET
   TRANSACTION READ WRITE`, `SET transaction_read_only = off`, `BEGIN READ WRITE`).
4. **The statement timeout.** A call at `read` or `diagnose` runs under `statement_timeout = '30s'`,
   and the client stops waiting after the same time. It bounds availability. It is not a security
   boundary, because a session could set it to 0; the policy refuses `set_config` and `SET`, which
   keeps the agent from doing so.

**The four layers that hold the guarantee at read and diagnose**

1. The database role decides what the connection may do at all. A statement in the session cannot
   switch it off.
2. The SQL policy parses every statement and checks it before it is sent.
3. The read-only transaction ends every call with ROLLBACK. It holds because the policy refuses the
   statements that would make the transaction writable.
4. The statement timeout stops a call after 30 seconds. It bounds availability and is not a security
   boundary.

After every call the connection goes back to the pool reset: `DISCARD ALL` releases advisory locks
and prepared statements, and the `hypopg` extension's hypothetical and hidden indexes are cleared. A
call can then not leave session state behind for the next one.

At `write` there is no policy and no timeout: the agent runs whatever the login may run, and the
database role is the only limit. This is why a `write` login should have only the grants the task
needs, and why the role gate does not apply to it.

## What each level's policy admits

|  | `read` | `diagnose` |
|---|---|---|
| Statements | SELECT without a locking clause, SHOW | The same, plus EXPLAIN with any options, ANALYZE included, when the explained statement passes the policy |
| Functions | A fixed list of functions for aggregates, math, strings, dates, JSON, arrays, catalog information and the like | The same list, plus `hypopg_create_index`, `hypopg_reset`, `hypopg_list_indexes`, `hypopg_relation_size`, `hypopg_get_indexdef`, `hypopg`, `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn`, `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn` and `pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp` |

Neither level admits the statements VACUUM and ANALYZE, CREATE EXTENSION, PREPARE and DEALLOCATE,
DECLARE, FETCH and CLOSE, or NOTIFY. Neither admits `pg_current_xact_id` (each call consumes a
transaction id), `gen_salt` and `crypt`, `ts_stat` and `ts_rewrite` (each executes SQL passed as an
argument), `set_config`, `pg_sleep`, or the `pg_advisory_*`, `lo_*` and `dblink*` functions.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE is refused before it reaches PostgreSQL, because
the explained statement has to pass the same policy. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a SELECT executes it, with
its full load, inside the transaction that is rolled back. The policy matches function names as
written, with a `pg_catalog.` prefix stripped, while PostgreSQL resolves the name through
`search_path`. It does not look at relations, operators or casts, so what the policy leaves open is
closed by the role and by the read-only transaction.

Every query text a tool sends starts with a marker comment, `/* dbwise read */`, `/* dbwise diagnose
*/` or `/* dbwise write */`, so a DBA reading `pg_stat_activity` can see which level sent it.

## What separates read from diagnose

The database role of each level's credential does, enforced by the role gate, together with the tool
split and the per-level statement and function sets. A `diagnose` role is a member of `pg_monitor`,
which shows other sessions' query text in `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_stat_statements`. A `read` role
should not be: the gate refuses it on an alias at `read`. On an alias at `diagnose`, every login is
checked at `diagnose`, so there it is the DBA's choice. PostgreSQL also grants some statistics
views, such as `pg_stat_user_tables`, to every role, so a `read` alias can query those. See
[Limitations](limitations.md#statistics-views-that-postgresql-grants-to-every-role-stay-visible-at-read).

## Why there are three SQL tools

`read_sql`, `diagnose_sql` and `write_sql` could be one tool whose effect depends on the alias. They
are three because Claude Code's permission rules match tool names. With three names you can allow
`read_sql` everywhere and keep `write_sql` on ask. One tool whose behaviour changed with the alias
could not be given that rule.

The tools that are not SQL tools follow the same rule. `list_schemas`, `list_objects` and
`get_object_details` are `read`; `explain_query`, `get_top_queries`, `analyze_db_health`,
`analyze_workload_indexes` and `analyze_query_indexes` are `diagnose`. A server registers a tool
only when at least one alias admits it, and each description starts with its level and the aliases
that admit it.

## Where the guarantee ends

- A server with `"role_check": "warn"` keeps the SQL policy and the read-only transaction and gives
  up the role layer, so it suits local and test databases. See
  [Limitations](limitations.md#a-server-with-role_check-set-to-warn-loses-the-role-layer).
- The role gate takes a snapshot when a pool opens. A grant made afterwards shows up after a
  reconnect.
- A view or a function that already exists in the database can do a lot of work inside the 30
  seconds a call has.

The full list is in [Limitations](limitations.md).
